context_blurb:
Sound, light, radio and the microwaves in an oven are all waves: travelling ripples that carry energy without carrying along the stuff they pass through. Waves add, cancel, echo, bend and bunch up, and people have put each habit to work.

A wave's speed is its frequency, the waves passing each second, times its wavelength, the distance from crest to crest. With the turntable out, a microwave oven melts spots in a chocolate bar half a wavelength apart, about 6 centimetres, so the waves are about 12 long. Multiply 12 centimetres by 2,450 million waves per second, the oven's frequency, and the result, about 294 million metres a second, is the speed of the microwaves. That is near light's speed: both are electromagnetic waves.

Overlapping waves add: crest on crest builds a bigger wave (constructive interference), and crest on trough, high point on low, cancels (destructive interference). In 1803 Thomas Young described splitting a narrow sunbeam with the edge of a card a thirtieth of an inch across. In its shadow, light from both sides overlapped in bright and dark bands. In each dark band, light from one side arrived half a wave behind light from the other, so the two met crest on trough and cancelled; blocking one side left nothing to cancel. Light plus light making darkness is what waves do, which told against Isaac Newton's particle theory.

Noise-cancelling headphones play a jet engine's drone back flipped upside down, so crest meets trough. Were the flipped wave to fall exactly half a wave behind, crest would meet crest, and the drone would sound louder than with the speaker off.

Waves also echo. After the Titanic sank in 1912, Paul Langevin in France built sonar, sending pulses of ultrasound, sound too high to hear, from quartz crystals that also caught the echoes; in 1918 trials it found a submarine over a kilometre away. Sound crosses sea water at roughly 1,500 metres each second, so an echo from an iceberg that returns in 4 seconds has gone six thousand metres there and back, and the iceberg lies half as far, about 3,000 metres away.

In 1955 the Glasgow doctor Ian Donald tested growths cut from his patients with a boilerworks' ultrasound flaw detector at Renfrew, beside a large steak. A cyst is a thin bag of fluid, and fluid has no boundaries inside it to send sound back. So the cyst echoed from its near wall, then fell silent until the pulse reached its far wall: echoes from those two walls only. A solid tumour's echoes weakened steadily with depth.

Radio waves echo too. In 1935 Arnold Wilkins and Robert Watson-Watt showed that a bomber miles away sends back a radio echo strong enough to catch, the start of radar. But sea water carries electric current, so it soaks up a radio wave's energy within a short way, a quarter of a metre or less, while sound crosses kilometres of sea.

Light bends, or refracts, on entering a material where it travels at a different speed. In 1966 the engineer Charles Kao argued that glass pure enough could guide light for kilometres. A fibre's core is wrapped in glass in which light travels a little faster. Light running down the core meets that boundary at too glancing an angle to cross, so all of it is reflected back in: total internal reflection, with no mirror needed. Purity did another job: Kao blamed the fibres' heavy losses on traces of iron and water soaking up the light.

In 1845, testing Christian Doppler's idea that motion changes the pitch heard, Christoph Buys Ballot had trumpeters hold one note on an open railway car, and people by the line heard it rise about a half-tone as the train neared. The trumpets never changed their note, and the air, not the train, set the sound's speed. But each crest set out from a little nearer the listener than the last, so the waves arrived bunched, more of them each second, and the note sounded higher.

Telephone cables need repeaters, stations that strengthen the fading signal and send it on. An analog call's smooth wave copies the voice, so each repeater amplifies the noise with it, and the hiss piles up. A digital call is a code of pulses, each either on or off. A digital repeater only has to decide which each pulse is, so it sends out fresh, clean pulses and drops any noise too small to change that answer.
